title:
Wang Yun deftly lays the double snare
Dong Zhuo rages at the Fengyi Pavilion
paragraphs:
Now [Kuai Liang](char-kuai-liang) said: "[Sun Jian](char-sun-jian) is dead and his sons are all young. Strike while they are weak. March at once, and [Jiangdong](loc-jiangdong) may be had at a single roll of the drums. Give back the body and break off the war, and you leave them time to grow strong, which will be the undoing of [Jing Province](loc-jing-province)." [Liu Biao](char-liu-biao) said: "[Huang Zu](char-huang-zu) is in their camp. How can I bear to leave him in their hands?" Kuai Liang said: "Why not give up one witless Huang Zu and take Jiangdong?" Liu Biao said: "Huang Zu and I are bosom friends. To cast him off would not be right." So he sent [Huan Kai](char-huan-kai) back to the camp, and it was agreed between them that Sun Jian's body should be exchanged for Huang Zu.
[Liu Biao](char-liu-biao) had [Huang Zu](char-huang-zu) back in exchange, and [Sun Ce](char-sun-ce) received [his father](char-sun-jian)'s coffin, drew off his army and went home to [Jiangdong](loc-jiangdong), where he buried him on the plain of [Qu'e](loc-que). When the mourning was done he led his army to [Jiangdu](loc-jiangdu) and settled there, calling the worthy to him, taking able men into his service, and bending his own pride to all who came, so that little by little the bold spirits of the four quarters gathered to him. But of that, no more here.
Now [Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo) was at [Chang'an](loc-changan), and hearing that [Sun Jian](char-sun-jian) was dead he said: "The thorn is plucked that in my bosom bred!" He asked how old the son was. Someone answered that he was seventeen, and Dong Zhuo thought no more of it. From that time he grew haughtier than ever. He styled himself Esteemed Father, and when he went out he usurped the pomp and escort of the Son of Heaven. His younger brother [Dong Min](char-dong-min) he made General of the Left and Marquis of Hu, and his nephew [Dong Huang](char-dong-huang) Palace Attendant with the whole command of the palace guards. Every man of the house of Dong, old or young, was made a full marquis. Two hundred and fifty li from Chang'an he raised a stronghold of his own, [Meiwu](loc-meiwu), and set two hundred and fifty thousand of the common people to build it. Its walls stood as high and ran as thick as the walls of Chang'an, and within were halls and storehouses with grain laid up for twenty years. He chose eight hundred young beauties out of the people to fill it. Gold and jade, colored silks and pearls were heaped there beyond all reckoning. His household lived within, and he came and went between Meiwu and Chang'an, now once in half a month, now once in a month, with the great officers waiting outside the Heng Gate to see him away.
[Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo) would often have a tent set up beside the road and drink there with the great officers. One day, as he went out by the Heng Gate with the whole court to see him away, he kept them to a feast, and just then some hundreds of soldiers from Beidi, who had laid down their arms on a promise of pardon, were brought up. Dong Zhuo had them dealt with in front of the company. The hands and feet of some were struck off, the eyes of some gouged out, the tongues of some cut away, and some were boiled in a great cauldron. The howling of them shook the sky, and the officials trembled till the chopsticks fell from their hands, while Dong Zhuo ate and drank, talked and laughed, quite at his ease.
Another day [Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo) called the whole body of officials together at the offices of state, and they sat in two long rows. The wine had gone round several times when [Lü Bu](char-lu-bu) walked straight in and said a few words in Dong Zhuo's ear. Dong Zhuo laughed. "So that is how it stands," he said, and bade Lü Bu drag [Zhang Wen](char-zhang-wen), the Minister of Works, from his place at the feast and down out of the hall. The officials paled. In a little while an attendant came in and presented Zhang Wen's head upon a red tray, and every man there sat half dead with fright. Dong Zhuo said, smiling: "Be easy, gentlemen. Zhang Wen was in league with [Yuan Shu](char-yuan-shu) and plotted to do me harm. A man carrying a letter between them delivered it by mistake at my son [Fengxian](char-lu-bu)'s house, and so I had Zhang Wen beheaded. You have done nothing, and need not be afraid." The officials murmured their assent and broke up.
[Wang Yun](char-wang-yun), Minister of the Masses, went back to his house turning over in his mind what had passed at that feast, and could not rest in his seat. Late at night, with the moon up, he took his staff and walked out into the back garden, where he stood beside the rose trellis and looked up to heaven, and the tears fell. Then he heard someone by the peony pavilion, heaving sigh after sigh. He crept up to look, and it was [Diaochan](char-diaochan), a singing girl of his own household. She had been chosen into the house as a child and taught to sing and dance. Now just sixteen, she was as skilled as she was fair, and Wang Yun treated her as his own daughter. He had listened a good while before he called out: "Wretch! Is this some love affair of yours?" Diaochan started and dropped to her knees. "How should I dare have any such thing!" Wang Yun said: "If there is none, what are you sighing for so late at night?" "Let me tell you what is in my heart." "Hide nothing. Tell me the truth of it." Diaochan said: "You have fed and reared me, sir, had me taught to sing and dance, and treated me better than I deserve. If my body were ground to dust I could not repay the least part of it. Of late I have seen your brows knotted with care, and knew there must be some great matter of state upon you, but I dared not ask. I sighed because tonight I saw again that you could neither sit nor stand at ease. I never thought you would be watching me. If there is any use you can put me to, I would not refuse it though it cost me my life." Wang Yun struck the ground with his staff. "Who would have thought the realm of Han should lie in your hands! Come with me to the painted chamber."
[Diaochan](char-diaochan) followed [Wang Yun](char-wang-yun) into the chamber. He drove out every maid and concubine, seated her, and knocked his head on the floor before her. She threw herself down in alarm. "Why do you do this, sir?" "Pity the living souls of Han!" said Wang Yun, and the tears came from him like water from a spring. "I said just now that I would not refuse any command of yours, though it cost me my life." Then Wang Yun knelt to her. "The people hang head downward, and ruler and ministers are no safer than eggs piled in a heap. There is none but you who can save them. The traitor [Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo) means to usurp the throne, and not a man at court has a plan against him. Dong Zhuo has a foster son, [Lü Bu](char-lu-bu) by name, of uncommon courage and strength, and both of them, as I read them, love women too well. So I would lay a double snare for them. First I shall promise you in marriage to Lü Bu, and then present you to Dong Zhuo. Between the two of them you must watch your chance, and contrive to set father and son at odds, until Lü Bu kills Dong Zhuo and the great evil is finished. If the altars of the land are propped up again and the state set on its feet, it will all be your doing. How does it seem to you?" Diaochan said: "I have told you I would not refuse death. Give me to them, and I shall know how to manage it." "If this leaks out, my whole house will be destroyed." "Have no fear of it, sir. If I fail this great cause, let me die under a thousand blades."
[Wang Yun](char-wang-yun) bowed his thanks to her. Next day he took some bright pearls out of the store of his house, had good craftsmen set them in a coronet of gold, and sent it secretly to [Lü Bu](char-lu-bu). Lü Bu was overjoyed, and came himself to Wang Yun's house to thank him. Wang Yun had a fine dinner made ready, and when Lü Bu came he went out to the gate to receive him, brought him into the back hall, and set him in the seat of honor. Lü Bu said: "I am no more than a general of the Chancellor's residence, and you, Minister, are a great officer of the court. Why show me courtesy so far beyond my place?" Wang Yun said: "There is no hero in the realm today but you, General. It is not your office I honor, but your gifts." Lü Bu was well content. Wang Yun pressed the wine on him with every courtesy, and never left off praising [Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo)'s goodness and Lü Bu's own, till Lü Bu laughed aloud and drank his fill. Then Wang Yun sent the servants away and kept only a few women to pour the wine, and when it had warmed them both he said: "Call the child in."
Presently two maids in green led [Diaochan](char-diaochan) out in all her finery. [Lü Bu](char-lu-bu) asked in surprise who she was. "My daughter Diaochan," said [Wang Yun](char-wang-yun). "You have been so good to me, General, beyond anything I deserve, that I count you no stranger but one of my own blood, and so I have let her come out to see you." And he bade Diaochan fill Lü Bu's cup. She carried the wine to him, and glances passed between them. Wang Yun, feigning drunkenness, said: "The child begs you to drink deep, General. My whole house leans upon you." Lü Bu asked her to sit, but she made as if to withdraw. "The General is my dearest friend," said Wang Yun. "Where is the harm in sitting down?" So Diaochan sat down at Wang Yun's side, and Lü Bu never took his eyes off her.
After a few cups more [Wang Yun](char-wang-yun) pointed to [Diaochan](char-diaochan) and said: "I would give this girl to you, General, for a concubine. Will you have her?" [Lü Bu](char-lu-bu) rose from his place and thanked him. "If that may be, I am yours to command." Wang Yun said: "One of these days I will choose a lucky hour and send her to your house." Lü Bu's joy was past all bounds, and his eyes kept turning to Diaochan, and she answered them with her own. The company broke up soon after. Wang Yun said: "I would have kept you the night, General, but [the Grand Preceptor](char-dong-zhuo) might grow suspicious." Lü Bu thanked him over and over and went away.
Some days later, in the council hall, [Wang Yun](char-wang-yun) saw [Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo), and noticing [Lü Bu](char-lu-bu) was not at his side, he bowed to the ground and made his request: "I beg you to turn your carriage aside to my humble house and dine there, Grand Preceptor, if it should please you." Dong Zhuo said: "If you invite me, Minister, I will come at once." Wang Yun gave his thanks and went home, where he set out every dainty of land and water, placed the seat in the middle of the front hall, laid brocade on the floor and hung curtains within and without. At noon the next day Dong Zhuo came. Wang Yun in his court robes went out to meet him, bowed twice and gave him greeting. Dong Zhuo got down from his carriage, and above a hundred mailed men with halberds crowded in with him to the hall and ranged themselves on either side. Wang Yun made his two bows at the foot of the hall, and Dong Zhuo bade them raise him and gave him a seat next his own. Wang Yun said: "Your virtue towers so high that not [Yi Yin](char-yi-yin) nor [the Duke of Zhou](char-duke-of-zhou) could come near it." Dong Zhuo was mightily pleased. The wine went round and the music played, and Wang Yun paid him every honor.
When it grew late and they were flushed with wine, [Wang Yun](char-wang-yun) asked [Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo) into the back hall, and Dong Zhuo sent his guards away. Wang Yun raised his cup in congratulation. "I have studied the stars a little since I was a boy, and watching the signs of heaven at night I find that the fated years of the house of Han are run out. Your merit and virtue shake the realm, Grand Preceptor, and were you to take the throne as [Shun](char-shun) took it from [Yao](char-yao), and [Yu](char-yu) from Shun, it would be what Heaven wills and men desire." Dong Zhuo said: "How should I dare look so high!" Wang Yun said: "It has been said from of old that he who has the Way strikes down him who has not, and he who lacks virtue gives place to him who has it. How should that be presumptuous?" Dong Zhuo said with a laugh: "If the mandate of Heaven does indeed come to me, you shall stand first in merit, Minister."
[Wang Yun](char-wang-yun) thanked him. Painted candles were lit in the hall, and none were left there but the serving women to bring the wine and the dishes. Wang Yun said: "The Imperial Music Office has nothing good enough to set before you. I have a singer of my own household, and make bold to bid her wait upon you." [Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo) said: "Very good." So Wang Yun had the blinds let down, the reed pipes wound their music round the hall, and [Diaochan](char-diaochan) was led out to dance beyond the blind. There is a lyric in praise of her:
> Born to the [Zhaoyang](misc-zhaoyang-palace) halls in days of old,
> A startled swan, a form one palm could hold.
> Across Lake Dongting, borne upon the breeze,
> She treads the Liangzhou measure through with ease,
> A fresh new blossom that the breezes swing;
> The painted hall's warm scent must yield to spring.
And a poem too:
> Quick flies the swallow to the clappers' call,
> A drift of cloud comes to the painted hall.
> Her dark brows the wanderer's grief impart,
> Her face at first sight breaks the old love's heart.
> No gold could ever buy a smile so rare;
> The willow's sash requires no gem to wear.
> Through the drawn blind they steal a parting view;
> And none can tell which man is [king of Chu](char-king-xiang-of-chu).
The dance done, [Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo) bade her come near, and [Diaochan](char-diaochan) stepped inside the blind and bowed low twice. Dong Zhuo saw her beauty, and asked: "Who is this girl?" [Wang Yun](char-wang-yun) said: "Diaochan, a singing girl of my house." "Can she sing for us?" Then Wang Yun bade Diaochan take the wooden clappers and sing a song. Truly:
> One cherry mouth unclosing, red lips sing,
> Two rows of jade breathe out the sunny spring.
> A tongue of clove spits out a steely blade,
> To cut the traitor down who wrecks the state.
[Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo) could not praise her enough, and [Wang Yun](char-wang-yun) bade [Diaochan](char-diaochan) fill his cup. Dong Zhuo raised it. "How old are you?" "I am just sixteen," said Diaochan. Dong Zhuo laughed. "Truly one of the immortals!" Wang Yun rose. "I would present this girl to you, Grand Preceptor, if you will take her." Dong Zhuo said: "How am I to repay such a favor?" Wang Yun said: "To wait upon you is more than she deserves." Dong Zhuo thanked him many times over. Wang Yun ordered a felt carriage made ready at once and sent Diaochan on ahead to the Chancellor's residence. Dong Zhuo rose and took his leave, and Wang Yun went with him the whole way to the residence before turning back. He had not ridden half the road home when he saw two rows of red lanterns lighting the way, and [Lü Bu](char-lu-bu) came riding up with his halberd in his hand. They met face to face. Lü Bu reined in, caught Wang Yun by the breast of his robe, and demanded fiercely: "You promised Diaochan to me, Minister, and now you have sent her to the Grand Preceptor. Do you make a fool of me?" Wang Yun cut him short. "This is no place to talk. Come to my humble house."
[Lü Bu](char-lu-bu) went with [Wang Yun](char-wang-yun) to his house, got down from his horse and came into the back hall. When the greetings were over Wang Yun said: "Why are you angry with this old man, General?" Lü Bu said: "I am told you sent [Diaochan](char-diaochan) to the Chancellor's residence in a felt carriage. What is the meaning of it?" Wang Yun said: "Then you have not heard it all, General! Yesterday in the council hall [the Grand Preceptor](char-dong-zhuo) said to me: 'I have a matter in hand, and I will come to your house.' So I made ready and waited for him. Over the wine he said: 'I hear you have a daughter called Diaochan, and that you have promised her to my son [Fengxian](char-lu-bu). I was afraid your word might not hold, and I have come on purpose to ask for her and see her.' I dared not cross him, and brought Diaochan out to make her bow to her father-in-law. Then the Grand Preceptor said: 'Today is a lucky day. I will take the girl home with me now and give her to Fengxian.' General, with the Grand Preceptor himself come to my house, how should this old man dare refuse him?" Lü Bu said: "Forgive me, Minister. I was mistaken for a moment, and tomorrow I will come and beg your pardon." Wang Yun said: "The girl has a little dowry, and when she has gone over to your house, General, I will send it after her."
[Lü Bu](char-lu-bu) thanked him and went away. Next day he made inquiries at the Chancellor's residence and heard not a word, so he pushed on into the hall and questioned the waiting-women. One of them answered: "The Grand Preceptor lay last night with his new lady, and is not risen yet." Lü Bu was in a fury. He slipped round behind [Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo)'s bedchamber to spy. [Diaochan](char-diaochan) had risen and was combing her hair below the window when she saw in the pool outside it the reflection of a man, tall and broad, with a coronet binding up his hair. She stole a look, and it was Lü Bu. She knit her brows on purpose and put on a sorrowful face, and wiped her eyes again and again with a scented silk. Lü Bu watched a long while, then went out, and in a little while came in again. Dong Zhuo was by now sitting in the middle hall, and seeing him come he asked whether all was well outside. Lü Bu said it was, and stood in attendance at his side. Dong Zhuo was at his food, and Lü Bu, watching out of the corner of his eye, saw a woman behind the embroidered blind going to and fro and peeping out, showing half her face and sending him her looks. He knew it was Diaochan, and his senses swam. Dong Zhuo saw the look of him, and grew suspicious and jealous. "If there is nothing to report, [Fengxian](char-lu-bu), you may go," he said, and Lü Bu went out sullenly.
From the day he took [Diaochan](char-diaochan), [Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo) was so bewitched by her beauty that for a month and more he never came out to see to any business. He fell slightly ill, and Diaochan nursed him night and day without once undressing, and bent herself to please him in everything, so that he grew fonder of her than before. [Lü Bu](char-lu-bu) came in to ask after his health and found Dong Zhuo asleep. Diaochan leaned half out from behind the bed and looked at Lü Bu. She pointed to her heart and then to Dong Zhuo, and the tears would not stop. Lü Bu's heart broke within him. Then Dong Zhuo's eyes opened dimly, and he saw Lü Bu staring fixedly behind the bed. He turned and looked, and there was Diaochan standing behind it. A great rage took Dong Zhuo, and he railed at Lü Bu: "You dare to toy with my own concubine!" He called his men to put him out, and forbade him the hall from that day on.
[Lü Bu](char-lu-bu) went home angry and brooding, and meeting [Li Ru](char-li-ru) on the road he told him the whole story. Li Ru hurried in to [Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo). "You mean to take the realm, Grand Preceptor. Why rebuke [the Marquis of Wen](char-lu-bu) for so small a fault? If his heart turns, the great design will be lost." Dong Zhuo said: "What is to be done?" Li Ru said: "Call him in tomorrow morning, give him gold and silk, and comfort him with kind words. The matter will settle itself." Dong Zhuo did as he was advised. Next day he had Lü Bu called into the hall and comforted him. "I was sick the other day and my wits wandered, so I spoke amiss and wounded you. Do not take it to heart." And he gave him ten jin of gold and twenty bolts of brocade. Lü Bu thanked him and went away, but though his body was at Dong Zhuo's side his heart was bound to [Diaochan](char-diaochan).
When [Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo) was well again he went up to court to deliberate, and [Lü Bu](char-lu-bu) attended him with his halberd. Seeing Dong Zhuo deep in talk with [the Emperor](char-prince-xie), he took his chance and carried the halberd out by the inner gate, got to horse and rode straight for the Chancellor's residence. He tied his horse before the gate, took the halberd into the back hall, and found [Diaochan](char-diaochan). She said: "Go and wait for me by the Fengyi Pavilion in the back garden." Lü Bu took the halberd and went, and stood below the pavilion beside the winding rail. After a long while Diaochan came, parting the flowers and brushing the willows aside, for all the world like an immortal out of the moon, and said to him weeping: "I am no true daughter of [Minister Wang](char-wang-yun)'s, but he treated me as his own. When I first saw you, General, and was promised to keep your house, my whole life's wish was granted. Who would have thought the Grand Preceptor would conceive a wicked desire and defile me? I longed to die on the spot, but I had never said farewell to you, and so I bore the shame and lived on. Now that I have seen you my wish is fulfilled. This body is fouled and may serve a hero no longer. Let me die before your eyes, and show you my heart!" With that she laid hold of the winding rail and sprang toward the lotus pool, but Lü Bu caught her in his arms and wept over her. "I have long known your heart! I grieved only that we could never speak together!" Diaochan clung to him. "In this life I cannot be your wife. Let us look to meet in the life to come." Lü Bu said: "If I cannot have you to wife in this life, I am no hero!" She said: "Every day I live is like a year. Have pity and save this girl." Lü Bu said: "I have stolen a moment to come here, and I fear the old traitor may suspect me. I must be gone quickly." Diaochan caught at his coat. "If you are so afraid of the old traitor, I shall never see the light of day again!"
[Lü Bu](char-lu-bu) stood still. "Give me time to think out a good plan." And with that he took up his halberd to go. [Diaochan](char-diaochan) said: "In my inner chamber your name came to my ears like thunder, General, and I took you for the man of the age. Who would have thought you served another!" And the tears fell from her like rain. Shame covered Lü Bu's face. He leaned the halberd aside again, turned and took her in his arms, and comforted her with soft words. The two clung close together and could not bear to part.
Now [Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo), in the hall of audience, turned his head and could not see [Lü Bu](char-lu-bu). Suspicion rose in him. He took a hurried leave of [the Emperor](char-prince-xie), got into his carriage and drove home, and there was Lü Bu's horse tied before the gate. He asked the gatekeeper, who answered: "[The Marquis of Wen](char-lu-bu) has gone into the back hall." Dong Zhuo sent his people away and went straight into the back hall, and found no one there. He called for [Diaochan](char-diaochan), and she was not to be seen either. He asked the waiting-women in haste, and they said: "Diaochan is in the back garden, looking at the flowers."
[Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo) went into the back garden and found them there, [Lü Bu](char-lu-bu) and [Diaochan](char-diaochan) talking together below the Fengyi Pavilion, with the halberd leaning at one side. In his anger he gave a great shout. Lü Bu saw him come and started back in alarm, then turned and ran. Dong Zhuo snatched up the halberd and came after him with it leveled. But Lü Bu ran fast, and Dong Zhuo was too fat to overtake him. So he hurled the halberd at him, and Lü Bu struck it down to the ground. Dong Zhuo picked it up and ran on, but by then Lü Bu was far away. As Dong Zhuo came out at the garden gate, a man came flying toward him and crashed against his chest, and down he went. Truly:
> His wrath rose up a thousand zhang on high;
> The fat bulk tumbled, in a heap to lie.
Who this man was, the next chapter will tell.

versions.name: Cheng Pu
versions.description: Style name Demou. A general of the Sun house, who served [Sun Jian](char-sun-jian) and now serves his son [Sun Ce](char-sun-ce); carries an iron-spined serpent spear.

versions.name: Diaochan
versions.description: A singing girl of [Wang Yun](char-wang-yun)'s household.

versions.name: Diaochan
versions.description: A singing girl of [Wang Yun](char-wang-yun)'s household, given by him to [Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo).

versions.name: Ding Yuan
versions.description: Style name Jianyang. Inspector of [Jing Province](loc-jing-province). Killed in his own tent by his foster son [Lü Bu](char-lu-bu).

versions.name: Dong Huang
versions.description: Nephew of [Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo), who made him Palace Attendant.

versions.name: Dong Min
versions.description: Younger brother of [Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo), who made him General of the Left and Marquis of Hu.

versions.name: Dong Zhuo
versions.description: Chancellor of State and Grand Preceptor, and master of the court.

versions.name: the Duke of Zhou
versions.description: Brother of King Wu, who founded the Zhou, and regent for King Wu's young son King Cheng. He put down the rebellion of his own brothers, settled the rites and institutions of the dynasty, and gave the government back when the boy came of age.

versions.name: Emperor Gaozu
versions.description: Personal name Liu Bang, founding emperor of the Han dynasty; rose from commoner origins to overthrow the Qin and establish the Han.

versions.name: Huan Kai
versions.description: An officer in [Sun Ce](char-sun-ce)'s army, and an old acquaintance of [Liu Biao](char-liu-biao)'s.

versions.name: Huang Zu
versions.description: Serves [Liu Biao](char-liu-biao), and commands the forces of [Jiangxia](loc-jiangxia).

versions.name: King Xiang of Chu
versions.description: A king of the old state of Chu. In legends he meets the goddess of Mount Wu in a dream; ever since, the story has stood for a meeting with a woman of more than mortal beauty.

versions.name: Kuai Liang
versions.description: Style name Zirou. Elder of the two Kuai brothers, who serve [Liu Biao](char-liu-biao) as advisers.

versions.name: Lady Wu
versions.description: Wife of [Sun Jian](char-sun-jian), and mother of his four sons [Sun Ce](char-sun-ce), [Sun Quan](char-sun-quan), [Sun Yi](char-sun-yi) and [Sun Kuang](char-sun-kuang).

versions.name: Li Ru
versions.description: Son-in-law and counselor to [Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo).

versions.name: Liu Biao
versions.description: Style name Jingsheng. Inspector of [Jing Province](loc-jing-province), and a member of the Han imperial house.

versions.name: Lü Bu
versions.description:
Style name Fengxian. Foster son of [Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo); killed his former foster father [Ding Yuan](char-ding-yuan).
Serves as Cavalry Commandant, General of the Household and Marquis of Wen.

versions.name: Lü Gong
versions.description: A general in [Liu Biao](char-liu-biao)'s service. Speared down by [Cheng Pu](char-cheng-pu) below [Mount Xian](loc-mount-xian).

versions.name: Emperor Xian
versions.description:
Previously Prince of Chenliu. Style name Bohe.
Set on the throne by [Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo) at the age of nine.

versions.name: Shun
versions.description: A sage emperor of high antiquity, raised from obscurity by [Yao](char-yao), who gave him the throne in place of his own son. He did the same in turn, passing it to [Yu](char-yu) over his own son.

versions.name: Sun Ce
versions.description: Style name Bofu. Eldest son of [Sun Jian](char-sun-jian) and [Lady Wu](char-lady-wu), and head of the house since his father's death.

versions.name: Sun Ce
versions.description: Style name Bofu. Eldest son of [Sun Jian](char-sun-jian) and [Lady Wu](char-lady-wu), and head of the house since his father's death. Settled with his army at [Jiangdu](loc-jiangdu).

versions.name: Sun Jian
versions.description:
Style name Wentai.
Marquis of Wucheng and Grand Administrator of Changsha.
Killed on [Mount Xian](loc-mount-xian) in [Lü Gong](char-lu-gong)'s ambush.

versions.name: Sun Jian
versions.description:
Style name Wentai.
Marquis of Wucheng and Grand Administrator of Changsha.
Killed on [Mount Xian](loc-mount-xian) in [Lü Gong](char-lu-gong)'s ambush, and buried at [Qu'e](loc-que).

versions.name: Sun Kuang
versions.description: Style name Jizuo. Fourth son of [Sun Jian](char-sun-jian) and [Lady Wu](char-lady-wu).

versions.name: Sun Quan
versions.description: Style name Zhongmou. Second son of [Sun Jian](char-sun-jian) and [Lady Wu](char-lady-wu).

versions.name: Sun Yi
versions.description: Style name Shubi. Third son of [Sun Jian](char-sun-jian) and [Lady Wu](char-lady-wu).

versions.name: Wang Yun
versions.description: Minister of the Masses, one of the [Three Ducal Ministers](misc-three-ducal-ministers).

versions.name: Yao
versions.description: A sage emperor of high antiquity, held up as the first model of good government. He passed over his own son and gave the throne to [Shun](char-shun), whom he raised from obscurity.

versions.name: Yi Yin
versions.description: Chief minister to Tang, founder of the Shang. When Tang's grandson Tai Jia proved unfit to rule, Yi Yin banished him to the Tong palace and governed in his stead for three years, restoring him to the throne once he had mended his ways.

versions.name: Yu
versions.description: Founder of the Xia, the first dynasty of China. He mastered the great flood by cutting channels to carry the waters away, and received the throne from [Shun](char-shun).

versions.name: Yuan Shao
versions.description:
Style name Benchu. Of the great Yuan house.
Marquis of Qi and Grand Administrator of [Bohai](loc-bohai). Holds [Ji Province](loc-ji-province).

versions.name: Yuan Shu
versions.description:
Younger brother of [Yuan Shao](char-yuan-shao); of the great Yuan house.
General of the Rear and Grand Administrator of Nanyang.

versions.name: Zhang Wen
versions.description: Minister of Works, one of the [Three Ducal Ministers](misc-three-ducal-ministers).

versions.name: Zhang Wen
versions.description:
Minister of Works, one of the [Three Ducal Ministers](misc-three-ducal-ministers).
Beheaded at [Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo)'s order.

versions.name: Bohai
versions.description:
A commandery of [Ji Province](loc-ji-province).
[Show on map](map:Bohai commandery)

versions.name: Chang'an
versions.description:
The old capital of Han, on the south bank of the Wei River far west of [Luoyang](loc-luoyang). [Gaozu](char-emperor-gaozu) made it his capital at the founding of the dynasty. [Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo) carried the court here from Luoyang and made it the capital again.
[Show on map](map:Chang'an city)

versions.name: the Han River
versions.description: The greatest of the Yangtze's tributaries, running southeast across [Jing Province](loc-jing-province) to join it.

versions.name: Ji Province
versions.description:
A Han province of the northern plain.
[Show on map](map:Ji province)

versions.name: Jiangdong
versions.description: The land south of the lower Yangtze, in the east of [Yang Province](loc-yang-province).

versions.name: Jiangdu
versions.description: A county of Guangling Commandery, on the north bank of the lower Yangtze, facing [Jiangdong](loc-jiangdong) across the water.

versions.name: Jiangxia
versions.description:
A commandery of [Jing Province](loc-jing-province) on the middle Yangtze.
[Show on map](map:Jiangxia commandery)

versions.name: Jing Province
versions.description:
A Han province of the central south.
[Show on map](map:Jing province)

versions.name: Luoyang
versions.description:
Capital of Han at the novel's opening. Burned and emptied by [Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo) when he carried the court west to [Chang'an](loc-changan).
[Show on map](map:Luoyang city)

versions.name: Meiwu
versions.description: A walled stronghold at Mei, on the Wei River west of [Chang'an](loc-changan).

versions.name: Mount Xian
versions.description: A hill outside [Xiangyang](loc-xiangyang).

versions.name: Qu'e
versions.description: A county on the south bank of the lower Yangtze, in [Jiangdong](loc-jiangdong).

versions.name: Xiangyang
versions.description:
A city on the south bank of [the Han River](loc-han-river), in the north of [Jing Province](loc-jing-province).
[Show on map](map:Xiangyang city)

versions.name: Yang Province
versions.description:
A Han province of the southeast, reaching from the lower Yangtze to the southern coast.
[Show on map](map:Yang province)

versions.name: Three Ducal Ministers
versions.description: The three highest-ranking civil officials of the Han court: the Grand Commandant, the Minister of the Masses, and the Minister of Works.

versions.name: Zhaoyang
versions.description: A Han palace, home to Zhao Hede, whose sister the Empress Zhao Feiyan was called Flying Swallow for her dancing.
